questions.q: What do RPO and RTO each define?
options: RPO defines how much data loss is acceptable in the worst case; RTO defines how long recovery is allowed to take
They are two names for the exact same recovery metric
RPO is about cost, RTO is about which team responds
RPO applies only to KQL Databases, RTO only to notebooks
questions.explain: "We have backups" isn't a plan on its own — these two numbers force a real conversation about cost versus risk.

questions.q: Which parts of a Fabric-based system are already effectively covered by earlier lessons in this course?
options: Fabric item definitions via Git integration, and the underlying Azure resources via Infrastructure as Code
The actual streaming event data itself, fully and automatically
Nothing from earlier lessons applies to disaster recovery at all
Only Power BI reports are covered, nothing else
questions.explain: What's genuinely still open is the actual streaming data itself, beyond a KQL Database's own retention window.

questions.q: Why isn't Delta's time travel (Databricks Lesson 21) a substitute for a real disaster recovery plan?
options: VACUUM eventually removes old file versions permanently, and time travel only covers what's inside the retention window — never a true regional outage or a lost workspace
Time travel doesn't actually work with Delta tables
Time travel requires a separate paid Azure subscription
Time travel is identical to a full backup strategy in every respect
questions.explain: It's a lightweight recovery tool for a bad write within history, not a substitute for real backup planning.

questions.q: What's the difference between Lesson 57's incident and a genuine disaster, according to this lesson?
options: An incident is something wrong within a system that's still fundamentally there; a disaster is when the system itself is gone or unreachable
They are exactly the same thing, just at different severity levels
A disaster is always caused by a bad deploy, same as an incident
Incidents only apply to data quality, disasters only apply to pipeline health
questions.explain: The response is different: one is mitigate-then-fix; the other is restore-from-what-was-deliberately-backed-up.

questions.q: Why does a tighter RPO or RTO almost always cost more?
options: Guaranteeing less data loss or faster recovery generally requires more redundant infrastructure and more deliberate preparation
Tighter RPO/RTO targets are always free to achieve with no tradeoff
RPO and RTO have no real relationship to cost at all
Cost only relates to Fabric Capacity SKUs, not to recovery planning
questions.explain: This is why RPO and RTO force a real conversation about cost versus risk, rather than defaulting to the tightest possible targets.
